Q: Adding Git-Bash to the new Windows Terminal A:

As an addition to the other answers: I noticed that Git Bash as installed by Git for Windows gives a MINGW64 shell, while the methods here give an MSYS shell (at least on my machine, in 2026). The main differences between these two are the PATH and a few other environment variables. To get almost the same environment as in the original Git Bash, set the MSYSTEM environment variable to MINGW64 before starting bash.exe. This is most easily done with a batch script.

Here is the batch file I'm using:

@echo off
set MSYSTEM=MINGW64
"C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\bash.exe" --login -i

Put this in, e.g., %USERPROFILE%\bin\git-bash.bat, and put cmd.exe /c %USERPROFILE%\bin\git-bash.bat in Settings -> your profile name -> Command line (the cmd /c gets rid of the notorious "Terminate batch job (Y/N)?" prompt on ctrl-C or an error exit).

One nice thing, now we have a batch file anyway, is that you can easily add some extra tweaks to your environment. For example, with Visual Studio 18 installed I created a profile "Git Bash for VS 18" pointing to a batch file %USERPROFILE%\bin\git-bash-VsDevCmd-18.bat with these contents:

@echo off
call "C:\Program Files\Microsoft Visual Studio\18\Professional\Common7\Tools\VsDevCmd.bat" -startdir=none -arch=x64 -host_arch=x64
set MSYSTEM=MINGW64
"C:\Program Files\Git\usr\bin\bash.exe" --login -i

The second line is mostly copied from the standard "Developer Command Prompt for VS 18" profile. Again, use cmd /c %USERPROFILE%\bin\git-bash-VsDevCmd-18.bat in the settings.

This makes for a really nice power-developer shell, in my opinion.

Addendum: if you do this, you may find that when you start a batch script that tries to use some of the standard Windows utilities like find or sort, it instead uses the MINGW64 utilities with the same names but that work very differently. A, somewhat ugly, workaround for this is to create batch scripts like %USERPROFILE%\bin\find.bat containing:

@"C:\Windows\System32\find.exe" %*

...and similar for the other utilities. MINGW will add ~/bin to the PATH if that directory exists, and the cmd.exe that executes the batch file will see the .bat files and run the Windows commands, but MINGW won't see them because of their extension, so you can still use the Unix tools from your cosy Unix shell prompt. The utilities with the same name but different function/interface, between Windows and MINGW as shipped with Git for Windows, are: expand, find, reset, sort, tar, timeout and whoami. Okay, Windows tar is essentially a port of Unix tar, you can probably exclude that one with impunity. This list may grow in later Windows versions.

I do admit that it's getting a bit hacky by now, but it appears to work fine for me.

Q: Why does musl ldconfig ignore standard directories? A:

Short: use /etc/ld-musl-*.path for that. Not Alpine's "ldconfig"

Musl's FAQ has an answer to your question: https://wiki.musl-libc.org/faq

Q: ANSI Color Escape Sequences Different Foreground and Background color with 256 colors A:

Here's how you do it. A key issue most people miss, is that you need to set the ANSI foreground (text color) before the ANSI background color.

# Foreground: Red (text) : \e[0;31m
# Background: Dark Gray  : \e[48;5;235m
echo -e "\e[0;31m\e[48;5;235m ABCD_1234 \e[0m"
  • Also note that: ANSI ESC = \e = \033 = \x1b.

Q: What does this passage from CLRS mean? A:

If f(n) is in O(1) + O(2) + ... + O(n)", it means that there is a sequence of constants C_i, such that f(n) <= C_1 * 1 + C_2 * 2 + ... + C_n * n.

This is not a useful statement, because there is no common bound on these constants. You could have C_i = i^3, for example, so f(n) could be Ω(n^4) or much worse.
